title: Block close: find your way
hookLine: many doors into prayer, all opening to the same house
tomorrow: Love, and do what you will

cards: Luke has already shown Jesus slipping away into the wilderness to pray, and once spending all night in prayer on a mountain.
Then one day, "as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased," one of them asks: "Lord, teach us to pray." Not teach us about prayer. Teach us to do it.
This whole block has walked through a house of prayer, room after room, each furnished by a different family of Christians.
Today there's no new room, just a practical question: of all the doors you've opened, which one will you keep using?

teach.b: Walk back through the rooms. The Benedictines: listen, the hours, the kitchen rota, tools treated like altar vessels.
The Orthodox way of the heart: the mind brought down into the heart, watchfulness at the door, the prayer rope. The Franciscans, with brother and sister creatures.
The Carmelites, with Teresa's four ways to water a garden and God among the pots and pans. The Ignatian way: imagine the scene, notice consolation and desolation. Celtic blessings for everything.
Anglican morning and evening prayer. Luther's advice to his barber, Reformed psalms and family worship. Anabaptist yieldedness, Quaker silence, Methodist class meetings, a covenant renewed.

And lately, louder rooms: hands raised in praise, a hand on a shoulder, a word weighed, bold prayer for the sick, the preacher calling and the people answering, testimony, a Taizé line sung over and over, Iona's prayers for justice, a shared table, a notebook and a walk.

None of these was invented as a sampler. Each belongs to a community and a whole life of faith, meant to be kept, not tried once. Benedict asked his monks to promise stability: stay put, and let the place shape you.
In John's Gospel, Jesus says: "Abide in me, and I in you."

Abide means stay, remain, keep living there. And when the disciples asked to be taught, Luke records no catalog of methods. Jesus said, "When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven," one prayer to keep.
So the block ends with a choice. Not the best way.

teach.h: ONE DOOR, EVERY DAY THIS MONTH.
teach.b: Your way, for now: one door you'll walk through every day this month, until it feels like a room you live in.

how: In Christian practice, a rule of prayer is something kept over time: a daily office, a rosary or prayer rope, a quiet time with the Bible, a weekly prayer meeting, sometimes with guidance from a pastor, priest or spiritual director.

o: a final test on every prayer tradition in the block
the end of a block: many ways tried, one chosen to keep

games.q: the disciples have watched Jesus pray, and one of them asks, "Lord, teach us to pray." what does he give them?
o: a long list of methods to try.
one prayer to say: Our Father.
silence, since prayer can't be taught.
games.why: "when ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven." he answers with one prayer to keep.

practice: Let the rooms of this block drift past without judging them, and notice which one you keep coming back to. Choose that one, and make it small and concrete: when, where, and for how long; five minutes is plenty.
If you pray, you can offer the choice to God.

wordCard.voice: Block close. The end of the block on traditions of prayer: many rooms walked through, and one way chosen to keep.

orig.note: Greek: to stay, remain, abide. John 15:4 uses a form of it: abide in me, and I in you.

carryVoice: Your line: one way, kept. One door, until it feels like home. Tomorrow, a new block begins: living it.
